Chapter 6: Recognizing and Transforming Games People Play
As we dig deeper into this framework, you’ll notice that not every conversation is as clear or conscious as you might expect.
A lot of the time, people fall into these repetitive, almost hidden patterns—they’re called “games.” But don’t let the word fool you.
These aren’t the fun kind of games. Instead, they’re predictable back-and-forth exchanges with a secret motive. Usually, they end up leaving someone—sometimes both people—feeling frustrated or hurt.
So, how do these games actually start? Well, it’s often with what seems like a totally innocent comment. But before you know it, things spiral into confusion or irritation. The big issue here? Folks aren’t really saying what they need or how they feel. Instead, they use roundabout ways to try to get those needs met—often without even noticing they’re doing it.
Take the game “Why Don’t You – Yes, But.” Maybe you’ve seen this in action. One person brings up a problem, others rush in with solutions, but every idea is shot down with, “Yes, but that won’t work because…” What’s really going on? The person isn’t looking for answers—they might just want some attention or to feel understood. The end result? Everyone’s annoyed, and nothing gets solved.
These games aren’t random; we actually pick them up early in life, usually as ways to deal with tough emotions or needs that went unmet. Sure, they help us feel like we have structure, get attention, or keep some control—but there’s a catch. Over time, these patterns keep us stuck in roles that don’t feel good and reinforce negative beliefs about ourselves and others.
So, how can you tell if you’re caught in a game? Here are a few signs to watch for:
You notice the same, unsatisfying outcomes popping up in certain relationships. Or maybe you get that weird sense of déjà vu during conflicts, like, “Here we go again.” And sometimes, your emotional reaction feels way bigger than the situation really calls for.
If you want to transform these games, you need your Adult state to take charge. That means stepping back and saying something like, “I notice we keep having this same argument.” Or, being brave enough to share what you actually need: “I want to feel heard, not just given advice.” Sometimes, it’s about gently refusing to play along—stepping out of that old script.
Changing these patterns can feel awkward or even scary at first. It shakes up habits you’ve probably had for years. But here’s the good news: when you break free, your connections become a lot more honest and satisfying.
Relationships stop being about winning or losing, and start being about truly understanding each other.
Every time you spot and step out of a game, you’re taking back your freedom to choose how you relate to people. This shift helps you move toward that “I’m OK – You’re OK” mindset and lets you build deeper, more Adult-to-Adult connections.
